JSXGraph response — editable freehand polynomial approximation
Draw a curve across \([0,1]\). JSXGraph simplifies the captured pointer samples to nine fixed-x adjustment points and fits a degree-five regression polynomial. After you move one blue point, all blue points are projected back onto the new red polynomial. Assessment uses dense samples of that polynomial.

increasing, allowing flat portions. After drawing, adjust the blue points as needed.
Their x-coordinates stay fixed; when you release a point, every blue point is
snapped onto the recomputed red degree-five polynomial that will be assessed.

section: AI feedback with reusable mini-machine context
text:
AI feedback with reusable mini-machine context
This example is adapted and translated from the mini-machine exercises.


Mini-machine number representation
The mini-machine uses the simplified floating-point format
\[
\boxed{S}\quad\boxed{EEE}\quad\boxed{MMMM},
\]
where:

\(S\) is one sign bit;
\(E\) is a three-bit exponent field;
\(M\) is a four-bit mantissa field;
the exponent bias is \(3\).

Only normalized numbers with \(E=1,2,\ldots,6\) are used. The bit patterns \(E=0\) and \(E=7\) are excluded, so this mini-machine ignores subnormal numbers, infinities, and NaNs.
A bit pattern represents the number
\[
(-1)^S\left(1+\frac{M}{16}\right)2^{E-3},
\]
where \(M\) is the integer value of the four mantissa bits.
For example,
\[
0\;|\;100\;|\;0110
\]
has \(S=0\), \(E=(100)_2=4\), \(e=4-3=1\), and \(M=(0110)_2=6\). Therefore,
\[
x=(1+6/16)2^1=2.75.
\]
To encode a representable number, first write it as
\[
\pm(1.MMMM)_2\,2^e.
\]
Then determine the sign bit, calculate the stored exponent \(E=e+3\), and write \(S\), \(E\), and \(M\) as bit fields.

title: Interactive examples

Extended regression page
The original all-in-one examples page remains available. It contains the large JSXGraph response examples and serves as compatibility coverage while the focused pages above provide the primary navigation.

title: AI feedback and learning context
text:
The Feedback button can request progressive hints from an OpenAI-compatible model. Credentials and model choice are stored only in the student’s browser. Ordinary answer checking does not require an AI service.
The extension sends the exact task, the student’s current work, private checker results, the current hint level, and the relevant learning context. It asks the model to preserve the document language and to return concise student-facing feedback without exposing internal reasoning.

title: AI feedback and learning context
text:
Provider compatibility
The model capability adapter uses a portable request body for unknown OpenAI-compatible providers. It adds low-reasoning controls only for recognised model families and retries once with the portable baseline if a provider rejects optional parameters. See the adapter design notes for the policy and known limitations.
